title: Not yours to finish
hookLine: Rabbi Tarfon: it is not yours to finish the work, nor are you free to stop (Pirkei Avot 2:16)

lines: A CATHEDRAL. A ROW OF OAKS.
cards: Some work is too big for one life. A cathedral raised stone by stone. A row of oaks planted for shade the planter won't sit in.
A cure. A fair city. A child raised into a future the parent won't see the end of.
Work that size offers two easy answers: try to do it all yourself, or decide it's hopeless and do nothing. A rabbi in the Mishnah turns down both, in a single sentence. Today: Pirkei Avot.

teach.h: THE DAY IS SHORT, THE WORK IS GREAT.
teach.b: First, the setting. Pirkei Avot, the Ethics of the Fathers, is a part of the Mishnah gathered from short sayings of the early rabbis. Two of Rabbi Tarfon's sayings sit side by side.

The first is a quick, urgent picture: the day is short, the work is great, the workers are sluggish, the reward is much, and the master of the house is pressing. It sounds like a busy workshop at closing time.
It's also a picture of a life. Second, the release.
Then Tarfon says: it is not upon you to finish the work. That's a mercy. No single person has to repair the whole world, end every injustice, or get every child grown and safe.
In the same breath he adds: but neither are you free to walk away from it. The release isn't permission to quit. You can't finish, and you can't stop.
Both halves, held together, the way a sabbath held work and rest together a few days ago.
Fourth, what that leaves: your part, a shift in a long relay.

This week's voices have been circling it: a garden tended before you came and after you go, a craftsman who teaches what he knows, an ant gathering for a season it may not see. Tarfon names the shape.
The whole isn't yours. The piece in front of you is.

how: Pirkei Avot is studied in Jewish communities as a book of ethics, and Rabbi Tarfon's saying is one people turn to when a task feels too large to finish.

o: the Mishnah's Ethics of the Fathers
the Five Books of Moses read in synagogue
a prayer book for the Sabbath evening meal

games.q: Rabbi Tarfon's picture — tap the pairs.

s: Rabbi Tarfon says you must finish the work
he says it is not upon you to finish it.
Tarfon says that since you can't finish, you may stop
in the same breath: neither are you free to walk away.
this saying is found in Pirkei Avot, part of the Mishnah
it's among Rabbi Tarfon's sayings in chapter two.

games.q: the work in front of you is too big to finish in your lifetime. what does Rabbi Tarfon say?
o: finish it anyway, at any cost.
it isn't yours to finish, nor are you free to stop.
games.why: Tarfon pairs the release with the duty: not yours to complete, and not yours to abandon.

practice: Bring to mind something huge you care about that you'll never finish alone, a family's healing, a neighborhood, the health of the earth, and let it be as big as it is.
Then, inside that bigness, find one small part that's yours this week, a call, an hour, a page, and hold it in mind until it's concrete. If you pray, you can hold it in your own tradition's words.
